title: SQL: transactions, ACID and isolation levels
seriesDescription: Joins, aggregates, window functions and CTEs, indexes and EXPLAIN, ACID and isolation, locking. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: ACID, savepoints, the isolation levels and anomalies (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew) in the SQL standard and in PostgreSQL MVCC, with retry on serialization failures.
source: PostgreSQL 16 documentation (transaction isolation, MVCC, explicit locking, asynchronous commit); Designing Data-Intensive Applications ch. 7; Jepsen/Hermitage isolation tables; Use The Index, Luke

questions.prompt: Match each ACID property to its meaning.

right.text: All statements of a transaction take effect, or none do
A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints
Concurrent transactions do not observe each other's partial work
Once committed, data survives a crash because the log reached stable storage
Every replica returns the same data at the same instant

questions.explanation: Atomicity is implemented with undo/MVCC and rollback, durability with the write-ahead log and `fsync`, isolation with MVCC or locks. Consistency also depends on you declaring constraints.

questions.prompt: In the SQL standard's table, match each anomaly to the lowest isolation level that prevents it.
questions.explanation: The standard defines the levels by which of the three phenomena they allow: READ UNCOMMITTED allows all, READ COMMITTED forbids dirty reads, REPEATABLE READ also forbids non-repeatable reads, SERIALIZABLE also forbids phantoms.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, match each problem to the lowest isolation level at which it cannot happen.

left.text: Overwriting a concurrently committed change after reading the old value in application code (read, then `UPDATE`)

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, so dirty reads never occur at any level. At READ COMMITTED the read-then-`UPDATE` cycle can still lose an update; at REPEATABLE READ the second writer fails with `40001` (could not serialize access due to concurrent update). Write skew is only stopped by SERIALIZABLE (SSI). The single statement `UPDATE t SET x = x + 1` is safe even at READ COMMITTED because the update waits and re-evaluates on the new row version.

questions.text: PostgreSQL makes COMMIT durable by flushing the {1} (write-ahead log) before acknowledging. Readers do not block writers because of {2}, which keeps several versions of a row. The default isolation level is {3}.
questions.explanation: Old row versions are cleaned up later by `VACUUM`. Oracle also defaults to statement-level read consistency; MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL READ UNCOMMITTED behaves exactly like {1}. A REPEATABLE READ transaction uses one {2} for its whole life and can fail with SQLSTATE {3} when it meets a concurrent update, so the application must {4} the transaction.
questions.explanation: `40001` is `serialization_failure` ("could not serialize access due to concurrent update"); `40P01` is `deadlock_detected`. Both are retryable.

questions.prompt: A counter row holds 10 at READ COMMITTED. Two sessions each run `SELECT value` (both read 10), compute `10 + 1` in application code and then run `UPDATE counters SET value = 11`. What is the value after both commit?
questions.explanation: Both writes store 11, so one increment is lost (the expected value is 12). Fixes: `UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1` (atomic), `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before the read, an optimistic version column, or REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE plus retry.

`ROLLBACK TO s` undoes rows 2 and 3 but keeps the transaction (and row 1) alive; row 4 is inserted afterwards, so rows 1 and 4 commit. Verified on PostgreSQL. Nested transactions in application frameworks are usually implemented with savepoints.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In PostgreSQL, REPEATABLE READ also prevents phantom reads, even though the SQL standard only requires that at SERIALIZABLE.
questions.reason: A PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ transaction reads from a single snapshot taken at its first statement.

whys.a: Correct: with one snapshot for the whole transaction, rows inserted later are never visible, so phantoms cannot appear.
whys.b: R is the mechanism that explains A.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation. It prevents dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads but not write skew. MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ differs (it uses locking reads and next-key locks).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: PostgreSQL never exhibits dirty reads, not even at READ UNCOMMITTED.
questions.reason: In PostgreSQL's MVCC design readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.

whys.a: R is a separate property of MVCC and does not explain why uncommitted versions are invisible.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but visibility rules (only committed versions are visible to a snapshot) are the reason for A.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: The standard allows an implementation to give stronger guarantees than the level requires. PostgreSQL maps READ UNCOMMITTED to READ COMMITTED.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Write skew can still occur at REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL.
questions.reason: At REPEATABLE READ, PostgreSQL takes shared locks on every row a transaction reads, so concurrent readers block each other.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so this option wrongly calls both statements true.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (checked with the on-call doctors example); R is false because snapshot reads take no row locks.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: Example: two on-call doctors each check "at least one other doctor is on call" and go off call. Both commit at REPEATABLE READ and nobody is on call. At SERIALIZABLE one transaction fails with `40001`. Alternatives: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the rows read, or a constraint.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: At SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL prevents anomalies by blocking conflicting transactions with table-level locks until the first one commits.
questions.reason: A SERIALIZABLE transaction in PostgreSQL may be aborted with `SQLSTATE 40001` and must then be retried.

whys.a: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: Correct: PostgreSQL uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which tracks read/write dependencies and aborts a victim instead of blocking; R is true.

questions.explanation: SSI is optimistic: low overhead when conflicts are rare, but every client must be ready to retry the whole transaction.

questions.prompt: Table accounts(id, balance). Write the SQL that moves 50 from account 1 to account 2 so that either both updates are applied or neither is.
questions.explanation: Add a `CHECK (balance >= 0)` constraint so an overdraft aborts the whole transaction. Updating in a consistent id order also avoids deadlocks between opposite transfers.

questions.prompt: In pseudocode, given a function `doTransfer()` that runs a whole transaction (`BEGIN ... COMMIT`) and fails with `SQLSTATE 40001` when serialization fails, write a loop of at most 3 attempts that retries only on that error and stops after the first success.
questions.explanation: In real code re-raise on the last attempt and add jittered back-off. The whole transaction must be retried, not just the failing statement, because its snapshot is gone.

questions.prompt: Which anomaly can still happen at REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL?

options.text: Write skew: two transactions read overlapping rows and update different ones.
options.why: Right: snapshot isolation does not detect this read/write dependency cycle.

options.text: Dirty read of another transaction's uncommitted change.
options.why: PostgreSQL never shows uncommitted data at any level.

options.text: Phantom read of rows that a concurrent transaction inserted after the snapshot was taken.
options.why: The single snapshot hides rows committed after it was taken.

options.text: Non-repeatable read of a row changed by a concurrent committed transaction.
options.why: The snapshot is fixed, so a re-read returns the same version.

questions.explanation: Concurrent updates of the same row do not slip through either: the second writer gets "could not serialize access due to concurrent update" (verified).

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about PostgreSQL MVCC and isolation.

options.text: An `UPDATE` writes a new row version; dead versions are reclaimed later by `VACUUM`.
options.why: Right: that is why long transactions cause bloat.

options.text: At READ COMMITTED every statement sees a fresh snapshot of committed data.
options.why: Right: two SELECTs in one transaction can return different results.

options.text: Plain readers do not block writers and writers do not block plain readers.
options.why: Right: that is the main benefit of MVCC.

options.text: REPEATABLE READ takes shared read locks that block concurrent writers.
options.why: Snapshot reads take no row locks.

options.text: PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE is implemented with classic two-phase locking.
options.why: It uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation, not 2PL.

questions.explanation: Long-running transactions are expensive in PostgreSQL because they pin old row versions and hold back `VACUUM`; keep them short.

questions.prompt: The C in ACID is guaranteed by the database engine alone, even when the schema declares no constraints.

options.why: The engine only enforces the rules you declare; without constraints it will happily store invalid data.
Right: the database enforces declared constraints (keys, CHECK, foreign keys), but the application defines what valid means.

questions.explanation: Atomicity, isolation and durability are engine properties; consistency is a joint contract between the schema and the application.

questions.prompt: Setting `synchronous_commit = off` in PostgreSQL can lose the most recently committed transactions after an operating-system or server crash, but it does not corrupt the database.

options.why: Correct: the commit returns before the `WAL` is flushed, so the last few transactions (up to about three times `wal_writer_delay`) may vanish, yet the database stays consistent.
Not so: PostgreSQL documents this setting as a durability-for-latency trade that risks losing recent commits, not corrupting data.

questions.explanation: Unlike `fsync = off`, which can corrupt the cluster, `synchronous_commit = off` only risks the tail of committed work. It can be set per transaction, so non-critical writes (events, logs) can skip the flush wait.

questions.prompt: Write the SQL that starts a transaction at REPEATABLE READ isolation, in PostgreSQL, and reads the balance of account 1 from accounts.

checks.label: starts a transaction at REPEATABLE READ

questions.explanation: `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL` must come before the first query of the transaction, so `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL ...` is the usual spelling. The snapshot is fixed at the first query, and the application must retry on `SQLSTATE 40001`.
